collection_title: Chapter 8: Simple Graphics and Image Processing
collection_intro: Short, ungraded practice checks for sections 8.1–8.2 of *Fundamentals of Python: First Programs*, 3e. Only your first try on each question counts toward your score, so answer before you peek.

checks.title: Turtle objects: state, interface and instantiation
checks.subtitle: Heading and pen state, absolute versus relative turns, creating an instance, interfaces, accessors and mutators, and the turtle's coordinate system
checks.intro: A turtle that draws the letter T perfectly can draw it sideways one line later, if you lose track of what it remembers. Six questions on an object's state and the methods that read and change it.
takeaways: An object's state is the set of values of its attributes at a moment. A turtle's position, heading, color, width and pen (up or down) decide what the next method call does, and most method calls change some part of that state and leave the rest alone.
`left` and `right` turn *relative* to the current heading (left is counterclockwise, so it increases the angle); `setheading` sets an *absolute* direction: 0 is east, 90 north, 180 west, 270 south.

A class's interface is its set of methods, documented by headers, arguments, return values and changes of state. Accessor methods such as `heading()` only report state; mutator methods such as `up()` or `goto()` change it.

questions.stem: A new turtle starts at home, facing east. What does this code print?

code.label: Python
code.text:
t = Turtle()
t.left(90)
t.forward(30)
t.left(90)
t.right(45)
print(t.heading())

options.feedback: Two left turns of 90 raise the heading from 0 to 180 (west), and the right turn of 45 lowers it to 135. Moving forward changes the position, never the heading.
This treats `left` as clockwise: 0 − 90 − 90 + 45 = −135, which is 225. In Turtle graphics the heading *increases* as the turtle turns left, which is why north is 90.
This counts only one of the left turns, perhaps because `forward(30)` seemed to reset the direction. Moving changes position but not heading, so both left turns still count.
That is the heading before the last line. `right(45)` is relative: it rotates the turtle from wherever it points now, so the final heading is 45 degrees less.

questions.hint: Which direction does the heading's number move when the turtle turns left, and does moving forward touch the heading at all?
questions.explanation: A turtle's heading is part of its state, measured in degrees counterclockwise from east. `left(d)` adds `d`, `right(d)` subtracts it, and movement methods change only the position. Tracing state one line at a time is the reliable way to predict a drawing.
questions.aside: Turtle graphics come from Logo, the children's language Seymour Papert and his colleagues created at MIT in the late 1960s. Python still ships a gallery of turtle programs: run `python -m turtledemo` to browse them, with the code beside each drawing.
questions.ref: Section 8.1, "Overview of Turtle Graphics" and Table 8-1 (p. 190)

questions.stem: What does this code print?

code.label: Python
code.text:
t = Turtle()
t.up()
t.setheading(270)
t.forward(40)
t.down()
t.left(90)
print(t.isdown(), t.heading())

options.text: `True 0.0`
options.feedback: The pen was lowered by `down()` after the move, so `isdown()` is `True`. Turning left 90 from south (270) brings the heading to 360, which is east again: 0.

options.text: `False 0.0`
options.feedback: `up()` lifted the pen, but `down()` lowered it again before the print. State holds the *latest* value of each attribute, not the first one set.
The arithmetic is right, but a heading is an angle: 360 degrees points the same way as 0, and the turtle reports headings in the range 0 up to (not including) 360.
This turns clockwise from south (270 − 90). A left turn is counterclockwise, which increases the heading: from south it points east.

questions.hint: Which method call was the last one to change the pen, and which way is a left turn from due south?
questions.explanation: `up()` and `down()` set one attribute of the turtle's state, and `setheading` sets the heading to an absolute direction regardless of the old one. Each later call works from the state the earlier calls left behind, and headings wrap around at 360.

questions.stem: After `from turtle import Turtle`, a student writes `t = Turtle` and then `t.forward(50)`, which fails. Written as `t = Turtle()`, the same code opens a window and draws. What is the difference?

options.text: Without the parentheses, `t` names the class itself; no constructor runs and no instance exists
options.feedback: The parentheses call the constructor, which manufactures and returns a new `Turtle` object with default attributes. Without them, `t` is just another name for the class.

options.text: Without the parentheses, Python creates a turtle but skips opening its drawing window
options.feedback: No turtle is created at all. `Turtle` alone is the class, like a blueprint; only calling it, `Turtle()`, instantiates an object (and opens the window).

options.text: `Turtle()` imports the turtle module a second time, which the `forward` method requires
options.feedback: Imports happen in `import` statements, not in constructor calls. The module was already imported; what was missing is an instance of the class.

options.text: The parentheses pass the default position and heading, which `forward` must be given
options.feedback: A constructor *can* receive initial values, but here it receives none and supplies defaults itself. The real difference is that a call happens at all, producing an object.

questions.hint: What does writing a name with `()` after it do in Python, and what is left if you write only the name?
questions.explanation: Objects such as numbers and strings are created from literals, but a class like `Turtle` must be instantiated explicitly with `<variable> = <class name>(<arguments>)`. That expression is a constructor: it resembles a function call, supplies defaults for any optional arguments, and returns a new instance of the class.
questions.ref: Section 8.1, "Object Instantiation and the turtle Module" (p. 192)

questions.stem: The book writes `drawSquare` using only Table 8-2, without ever reading the code inside the `Turtle` class. What makes that possible?

options.text: The class's interface: its method headers and documentation of arguments, results and state changes
options.feedback: An interface contains just enough information to use objects of a class. Knowing that `goto(x, y)` moves the turtle and `down()` lowers the pen is all `drawSquare` needs.

options.text: `help(Turtle)` displays the code inside each method, so the table merely repeats it
options.feedback: `help` displays docstrings, the documentation of each method, not the code that implements it. That documentation is part of the interface, and it is designed to be enough.

options.text: The turtle's state: knowing its position, heading and color lets you predict every method
options.feedback: State is the current values of the attributes. Knowing them is useless without knowing which methods exist and what they do to that state, which is the interface.

options.text: Turtle methods are ordinary functions that never depend on the object they are called on
options.feedback: They depend heavily on the object: `forward` draws or not depending on that turtle's pen. You can use them without their code because the interface documents those effects.

questions.hint: What does Table 8-2 actually list for each entry, and what does it leave out?
questions.explanation: The set of a class's methods is its interface, and programmers interact with objects through it. A good interface documents each method's header, arguments, return value and effect on the object's state, and nothing about how it is implemented. `help(Turtle)` and `dir(Turtle)` show it at the shell.

questions.stem: Which group contains **only** accessor methods?

options.text: `t.position()`, `t.heading()`, `t.isdown()`
options.feedback: Each of these returns the value of an attribute and changes nothing, so calling them in any order leaves the turtle exactly as it was.

options.text: `t.home()`, `t.position()`, `t.heading()`
options.feedback: `home()` takes no arguments and returns nothing interesting, but it moves the turtle to the center and points it east. Changing state makes it a mutator.

options.text: `t.up()`, `t.down()`, `t.isdown()`
options.feedback: `isdown()` only reports, but `up()` and `down()` change whether the pen touches the surface: they are mutators, even though they take no arguments.

options.text: `t.width(2)`, `t.pencolor("red")`, `t.heading()`
options.feedback: `heading()` is an accessor, but given arguments, `width` and `pencolor` set the pen's width and color. A method that alters an attribute is a mutator.

questions.hint: Ignore whether a method takes arguments. For each call, ask: is the turtle any different afterwards?
questions.explanation: Mutator methods change an object's internal state (position, heading, color, pen); accessor methods only return values of its attributes. Having no arguments does not make a method an accessor: `home()` and `up()` change the turtle. Some methods, such as `width` and `pencolor`, are both: with no argument they report the current value.
questions.aside: Python's own built-in types follow the same split. A list's `count` and `index` methods are accessors; `append` and `sort` are mutators, and they return `None` precisely to remind you that they changed the list instead of making a new one.

questions.stem: With the book's `turtle.cfg`, the window is 300 by 200 pixels. Where does `t.goto(-150, 100)` send the turtle?

options.text: To the window's upper-left corner
options.feedback: Turtle graphics use Cartesian coordinates with the origin at the center. Half the width to the left (x = −150) and half the height up (y = 100) is the upper-left corner.

options.text: To the window's lower-left corner
options.feedback: This treats a larger y as lower on the screen, the convention for image pixels. In the turtle's Cartesian system, positive y is up, as on a graph.

options.text: Off the left edge of the window, since a window has no negative x values
options.feedback: That holds when (0, 0) is a corner. A turtle's home (0, 0) is the center, so negative x values are simply the window's left half.

options.text: To the window's upper-right corner
options.feedback: This pairs the 150 with the right side. The minus sign on x means left of the origin; it is y = 100 that means up.

questions.hint: Where is the turtle's home, (0, 0), and which way does a positive y point?
questions.explanation: A turtle moves in the standard Cartesian plane: (0, 0) is the center of the window, x grows to the right and y grows upward. That is why the book locates the corners with `window_width() // 2` and `window_height() // 2` and their negatives.
questions.ref: Section 8.1, "Overview of Turtle Graphics" (p. 190) and "Manipulating a Turtle's Screen" (p. 196)

checks.title: Shapes, patterns, RGB color and fractals
checks.subtitle: Shape functions that use the turtle's state, turn angles, passing a function as an argument, RGB intensities, bits per color, and the c-curve
checks.intro: Ten hexagons in a ring, a fill color out of 16 million, and a curve that keeps growing more detail: each comes from a few lines of code. Six questions on how.
takeaways: A shape function that starts from the turtle's current position and heading can be placed and rotated by its caller, so it can be reused inside larger patterns. A regular polygon with n sides turns 360 / n degrees at each corner.
In RGB, each of red, green and blue is an intensity from 0 (absent) to 255 (full). N bits store 2ᴺ values, so 8 bits per component and 24 bits per pixel give 256³ = 16,777,216 colors.
A recursive drawing replaces each piece with smaller copies of itself. In the c-curve, each level splits every segment into two, so a level-N c-curve draws 2ᴺ line segments.

questions.stem: `drawSquare(t, x, y, length)` moves to (x, y) and points south before drawing; `square(t, length)` just draws from wherever the turtle is. Why does `radialHexagons` use the `square`/`hexagon` style?

options.text: It starts from the turtle's own position and heading, so the caller can rotate it between shapes
options.feedback: `radialHexagons` turns the turtle by 360 / n between calls. Because `hexagon` begins at the current heading, each copy comes out rotated, which is what makes the ring.

options.text: It has fewer parameters, so Python runs it faster in a loop with many shapes
options.feedback: Two fewer arguments make no meaningful difference to speed. The gain is in design: the shape uses state the turtle already has instead of overriding it.

options.text: It lifts the pen before moving, so no stray lines join one shape to the next
options.feedback: That describes `drawSquare`, which calls `up()` and `goto`. `square` never lifts the pen: it simply draws from the current spot.

options.text: It returns the turtle to its home position afterwards, so each shape starts in the same place
options.feedback: Neither function calls `home()`. In fact, starting every shape at the same fixed spot and direction is exactly the limitation the new design removes.

questions.hint: What does the turtle already know that `drawSquare` throws away by calling `goto` and `setheading`?
questions.explanation: The book names two limitations of `drawSquare`: the caller must supply a location the turtle already has, and the shape always has the same orientation. Letting the shape start from the turtle's current position and heading makes it composable: any pattern can position and rotate the turtle and then call it.

questions.stem: Generalising `square` (turn 90, four times) and `hexagon` (turn 60, six times), a student writes `polygon(t, sides, length)`. What should the loop pass to `t.left` at each corner?

options.text: `360 / sides`
options.feedback: The turtle makes one full turn, 360 degrees, over the whole trip around the shape, split evenly among the corners: 90 for a square, 60 for a hexagon, 45 for an octagon.
That is the polygon's *interior* angle (120 for a hexagon). The turtle turns by the *exterior* angle, how far it changes direction, which is what's left of 180.

options.text: `180 / sides`
options.feedback: This gives 45 for a square, half the needed turn; the shape would not close. A complete trip around any closed shape turns the turtle through 360 degrees, not 180.

options.text: `sides * 90 / 4`
options.feedback: This fits the square (90) but gives 135 for a hexagon instead of 60. A formula built from one example has to be checked against the other.

questions.hint: After the turtle has gone all the way around the shape, how far has it turned in total?
questions.explanation: Drawing a closed regular polygon, the turtle ends facing the way it started, having turned through one full circle. Each of the n corners therefore turns 360 / n degrees. The same reasoning gives the `360 / n` turn between shapes in `radialPattern`.
questions.ref: Section 8.1, "Drawing Two-Dimensional Shapes" (pp. 194–195) and Exercise 8-1, question 4

questions.concept: Passing a function as an argument
questions.stem: The book calls `radialPattern(t, n = 10, length = 50, shape = square)`. A student writes the call below instead. What happens?

code.label: Python

options.text: One square is drawn, then a `TypeError`: `None` is not callable
options.feedback: `square(t, 50)` runs first, as an argument, drawing one square and returning `None`. Inside the loop, `shape(t, length)` then tries to call `None`.

options.text: Ten squares are drawn in a ring, exactly as when passing `square`
options.feedback: The parentheses make the difference. `square` hands over the function; `square(t, 50)` calls it immediately and hands over its result, which is `None`.

options.text: A `SyntaxError`, because a function call cannot appear as an argument
options.feedback: Calls as arguments are legal and common, as in `print(len(s))`. The code runs; the problem is the *value* the call produces.

options.text: Ten squares are drawn, but all on top of one another at the same angle
options.feedback: That would need `square` to run ten times. It runs once, before `radialPattern` starts, and the loop fails on its first pass.

questions.hint: Python evaluates every argument before the function receives it. What value does `square(t, 50)` produce?
questions.explanation: A function's name refers to the function itself, which can be passed and called later; the name with parentheses calls it right away and passes its return value. `radialPattern` needs the function, because it calls `shape(t, length)` ten times, once per pattern element.

questions.stem: An early color display could show 64 distinct colors. At minimum, how many bits of memory did each pixel need?

options.feedback: N bits represent 2ᴺ values, and 2⁶ = 64. With 5 bits there would be only 32 colors; with 7, 64 would leave half the patterns unused.
This is the number of values, not the number of bits. Each extra bit doubles the count, so 64 bits could distinguish about 18 quintillion colors.
Eight bits, one byte, is the size of one RGB component, and it gives 256 values. For only 64 colors, two of those bits would be wasted.
This halves the number of colors. Bits and values are related by powers of two, not by division: N distinct values need log₂N bits.

questions.hint: How many values can 1 bit store? 2 bits? 3 bits? Keep doubling.
questions.explanation: N bits of memory can represent 2ᴺ distinct values, and N distinct values need at least log₂N bits. That is how the book gets from 1 bit for black and white, to 3 bits for eight grays, to 24 bits and 16,777,216 colors for true-color RGB.
questions.aside: Web colors use the same 24 bits. In a hex code such as `#FF8000`, each pair of hex digits is one RGB component from 00 to FF, that is, 0 to 255: this one is (255, 128, 0), an orange.

questions.stem: A program changes a pixel from `(255, 0, 0)` to `(127, 0, 0)`. What does the viewer see?

options.text: A darker red, because red is now about half its full intensity
options.feedback: Each component is an intensity: 255 is maximum saturation and 0 is total absence. Halving red, with no green or blue, moves the color halfway toward black.

options.text: A paler red, closer to pink, because the color is now less saturated
options.feedback: Pale colors come from *adding* the other components, toward white (255, 255, 255). Lowering red with green and blue at 0 moves toward black, (0, 0, 0).

options.text: A mid gray, because 127 is the middle value of every component
options.feedback: Gray needs all three components equal, as in (127, 127, 127). Here green and blue stay at 0, so the pixel is still pure red, only dimmer.

options.text: The same red: the eye cannot tell adjacent RGB values apart
options.feedback: That is true of neighbouring values such as 254 and 255. A drop of 128 steps is far from adjacent, and it is easy to see.

questions.hint: In RGB, what does 0 in a component mean, and what color has all three components at 0?
questions.explanation: RGB mixes three integer intensities, each from 0 (absent) to 255 (full). Lowering a component dims that light; raising all three together lightens a color toward white; equal components give a shade of gray. Table 8-3 shows the anchors: black (0, 0, 0), white (255, 255, 255), gray (127, 127, 127).
questions.ref: Section 8.1, "Colors and the RGB System" and Table 8-3 (p. 197)

questions.stem: This is the case study's `cCurve`, with `drawLine` replaced by a counter. What does it print?

code.label: Python
code.text:
count = 0

def cCurve(x1, y1, x2, y2, level):
    global count
    if level == 0:
        count += 1    # stands in for drawLine
    else:
        xm = (x1 + x2 + y1 - y2) // 2
        ym = (x2 + y1 + y2 - x1) // 2
        cCurve(x1, y1, xm, ym, level - 1)
        cCurve(xm, ym, x2, y2, level - 1)

cCurve(50, -50, 50, 50, 4)
print(count)

options.feedback: Each level replaces every segment with two half-size ones, so the number of segments doubles per level: 1, 2, 4, 8, then 16 at level 4.
This is the count for level 3. The recursion stops at level 0, not level 1, so there are four doublings from the top call, not three.
That is the number of *calls*, 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16. Only the calls that reach the base case draw a segment; the others just split the work.
This counts the levels, as if each level drew one segment. A level draws nothing itself: it makes two calls one level lower.

questions.hint: How many segments does a level-0 curve draw, and how many does a level-1 curve draw?
questions.explanation: A recursive pattern of this shape, two recursive calls per level and work only at the base case, does 2ᴺ pieces of work at level N. That is why a level-10 c-curve has 1,024 segments, and why the program turns off animation with `tracer(False)` when the level is above 8.
questions.aside: The c-curve is also called the Lévy C curve, after the French mathematician Paul Lévy, who studied its self-similarity in 1938. Zoom into any part of a high-level c-curve and you find smaller c-curves, which is the self-similarity that makes it a fractal.

checks.title: Digital images: sampling, formats and grids
checks.subtitle: Analog versus digital, how many pixels, lossless and lossy compression, screen coordinates, traversal order and tuples
checks.intro: A photo of a cat becomes 29,502 numbered dots, each with three numbers. Six questions on how that happens and how a program walks through them.
takeaways: Digitizing samples a continuous (analog) scene at discrete points on a grid and stores a color value for each. More samples per inch means more pixels and a more realistic image, at the cost of a larger file.

Lossless compression lets the original values be restored exactly; lossy compression approximates some of them. GIF keeps a palette of at most 256 colors, which suits flat areas but not smooth photographic shading.

Image pixels use screen coordinates: (0, 0) is the upper-left corner, y grows downward, and the last pixel is (width − 1, height − 1). A row-major traversal uses y in the outer loop and x in the inner loop.

questions.stem: A flatbed scanner turns a printed photograph into a digital image. What is it doing?

options.text: Measuring a discrete color value at each point of a two-dimensional grid
options.feedback: The photo's colors vary continuously; the scanner samples them at distinct points and stores one value per point. Those values are the pixels.

options.text: Recording the photo's continuous colors exactly, the way a record's groove follows the sound
options.feedback: That is how analog media work: a groove or film directly mirrors a continuous wave. A computer can only store discrete values, so it must sample.

options.text: Compressing the photo into a JPEG file so it fits in memory
options.feedback: Compression can happen afterwards, when the image is stored. Before there is anything to compress, the continuous scene must be turned into numbers.

options.text: Replacing each color with the closest of 256 palette colors
options.feedback: That is the second phase of GIF compression, a storage decision. Scanning itself produces a full color value for each sampled point.

questions.hint: A computer can only store discrete values. What has to happen to a continuous range of colors first?
questions.explanation: Images, sound and most of the physical world carry analog information: a continuous range of values. Digitizing maps it onto discrete values by sampling, measuring at distinct points on a grid. With enough samples, the digital image is nearly indistinguishable from the original scene.
questions.ref: Section 8.2, "Analog and Digital Information" and "Sampling and Digitizing Images" (p. 204)

questions.stem: The book uses 250 pixels per linear inch (62,500 per square inch). How many pixels does a 2-inch by 4-inch photo need at that density?

options.feedback: Along the sides that is 2 × 250 = 500 and 4 × 250 = 1,000 pixels, and 500 × 1,000 = 500,000. Equivalently, 8 square inches × 62,500.
This multiplies the area, 8 square inches, by the *linear* density, 250. Pixels per inch counts along one edge; an area needs pixels per square inch.
This scales only one side, 4 inches × 62,500. The square-inch figure already covers both directions, so it should be multiplied by the full area, 8.
This is the book's 3-by-5 example rounded up to a megapixel. A 2-by-4 photo is about half as large in area, so it needs about half as many pixels.

questions.hint: Count pixels along each side first, then combine them.
questions.explanation: A sampling density is given per linear unit, so the number of pixels grows with the *square* of the density: doubling pixels per inch quadruples the total. The book's 3-by-5-inch photo at 250 pixels per inch needs 937,500 pixels, about one megapixel.

questions.stem: A web page needs (a) a banner logo with large flat areas in five colors and (b) a photo of a sunset with smooth color gradients. For which is GIF a good fit?

options.text: The logo, because its few flat colors fit comfortably in a 256-color palette
options.feedback: GIF stores up to 256 prevalent colors and a palette key per pixel. Five flat colors lose nothing that way, while a gradient's thousands of shades must be forced onto 256.

options.text: The photo, because GIF is a lossless format that keeps every original color
options.feedback: GIF is lossy: every pixel is replaced by the key of the closest palette color. That loss is invisible for a few flat colors and visible as banding in a gradient.

options.text: Both equally, since the human eye cannot detect what compression removes
options.feedback: That holds for well-tuned lossy schemes in many photos, but 256 colors cannot cover a sunset's smooth shading, and the steps between shades can show.

options.text: Neither, because GIF can only store grayscale images
options.feedback: Gray is not required: the palette holds up to 256 colors of any kind. The limit is how *many* colors, not which ones.

questions.hint: How many distinct colors can a GIF hold, and roughly how many does each image contain?
questions.explanation: A raw file keeps every sample and is largest. JPEG combines lossless steps (restoring repeated values exactly) and lossy ones (approximating regions). GIF builds a palette of at most 256 colors and stores each pixel as a key into it, so it is lossy and works best on broad flat areas such as cartoons, backgrounds and banners.
questions.aside: GIF was introduced by CompuServe in 1987. Its palette of 256 colors is also why an animated GIF made from a video often shows visible bands or speckles: every frame has to be squeezed into at most 256 colors.

questions.stem: `smokey.gif` is 198 pixels wide and 149 pixels high. What are the coordinates of its lower-right pixel?

options.feedback: Coordinates start at 0, so the columns are 0 to 197 and the rows 0 to 148. The lower-right pixel is (width − 1, height − 1).
These are the dimensions, not a position. Counting from 0, a width of 198 means the last column is 197, as with the last index of a list.
This uses the turtle's Cartesian system, origin at the center and y up. Image pixels use screen coordinates: origin at the upper-left, y growing down.
This gives row first, then column. The book's coordinates are (x, y), that is (column, row), matching `getPixel(x, y)`.

questions.hint: Where is (0, 0) in an image, and what is the largest index in a range of 198 values?
questions.explanation: When an image is displayed, its pixels form a grid from (0, 0) at the upper-left corner to (width − 1, height − 1) at the lower-right. This screen coordinate system differs from Turtle graphics, whose origin is the center of the window and whose y axis points up.

questions.stem: This nested loop has `x` on the outside. What does it print?

code.label: Python

options.feedback: The inner loop runs completely for each value of the outer one. With `x` outside, it walks down each column (y = 0, 1) before moving right: a column-major traversal.
This is the row-major order from the book, which puts `y` in the outer loop. Here `x` is outer, so `x` changes slowest.
This is the book's 2-by-3 example, with width and height swapped. Here `x` takes three values and `y` two, so no pair has a `y` of 2.
This starts counting at 1. `range(width)` starts at 0, which matches the grid: the first pixel is (0, 0).

questions.hint: Which variable finishes its whole range before the other changes once?
questions.explanation: A nested loop visits every position of a grid: the outer loop fixes one coordinate while the inner loop runs through all values of the other. With `y` outside (row-major), each row is crossed before moving down; with `x` outside (column-major), each column is walked down before moving right. Both visit every pixel once.
questions.ref: Section 8.2, "A Loop Pattern for Traversing a Grid" (p. 208) and Exercise 8-2, question 5

questions.stem: A student wants `average` to unpack its pixel directly in the header. What happens when Python reads this definition?

code.label: Python
code.text:
def average((r, g, b)):
    return (r + g + b) // 3

options.text: A `SyntaxError`: a parameter must be a single name
options.feedback: Patterns like `(r, g, b)` work in assignments, but a parameter must be a plain name. The book's version takes `triple` and unpacks it in the body.

options.text: It works: `average((40, 50, 60))` returns `50`
options.feedback: That is the result of the book's correct version. Unpacking in the header is not allowed, so the definition never gets as far as being called.

options.text: It defines the function, then raises `TypeError` when called with one tuple
options.feedback: This imagines Python reading the header as three parameters. The error comes earlier: the header itself is invalid, before any call happens.

options.text: It works, but returns a tuple of three averages instead of one number
options.feedback: `(r + g + b) // 3` is one integer either way. The problem is not the body; Python rejects the header before running anything.

questions.hint: The book says tuple patterns work almost anywhere, with one exception. Which?
questions.explanation: Tuple assignment binds each element of a tuple to its own variable, as in `(r, g, b) = image.getPixel(x, y)`. It works almost anywhere except in a function's parameter list, where each parameter must be a single name; the function unpacks the tuple in its body.
questions.aside: Python 2 did allow `def average((r, g, b)):`. The feature was removed in Python 3 by PEP 3113, partly because they complicated tools that inspect a function's parameters, while giving little benefit over unpacking in the body.

checks.title: Image algorithms: transform, copy, blur and shrink
checks.subtitle: Black and white, weighted grayscale, clone versus an alias, why blur reads from a copy, and how shrinking reduces pixels
checks.intro: Every filter in a photo app comes down to a nested loop, a getPixel and a setPixel. Six questions, half of them traces, on the decisions that make those loops right.
takeaways: Some algorithms transform each pixel in place from its own values (black and white, grayscale); others read a source image and build a new one (blur, edge detection, shrink).

`clone()` makes a structurally equivalent but separate image, so changes to one do not affect the other; assignment only gives the same image a second name. An algorithm that reads neighbors must read from an unchanged source.
Grayscale weights green (.587) more than red (.299) and red more than blue (.114) because that is how the eye perceives luminance. Shrinking both dimensions by a factor N leaves 1/N² of the pixels.

questions.stem: This is the book's `blackAndWhite`, applied to a two-pixel image. What does the last line print?

code.label: Python

options.feedback: The first pixel averages (90 + 120 + 160) // 3 = 123, under 128, so it turns black. The second averages 400 // 3 = 133, so it turns white.
This decides by the brightest component: both pixels have one value above 128. The function compares the *average* of all three components with 128.
This swaps the two outcomes, perhaps by judging the bluish pixel as lighter. The rule is numeric: an average below 128 becomes black, otherwise white.
These are the averages, the grayscale-style result. `blackAndWhite` uses the average only to choose between two pixels, pure black or pure white.

questions.hint: Compute each pixel's average with `//`, then compare it with 128.
questions.explanation: Converting to black and white visits every pixel with a row-major nested loop, averages its three components, and replaces the pixel with black if the average is closer to 0 or white if it is closer to 255. It changes the argument image itself and returns nothing.
questions.ref: Section 8.2, "Converting an Image to Black and White" (pp. 209–210)

questions.stem: These lines are the body of the book's `grayscale` loop, applied to one pixel. What do they print?

options.feedback: Each product is truncated *before* adding: `int(29.9)` is 29, `int(117.4)` is 117 and `int(5.7)` is 5, and 29 + 117 + 5 = 151.
29.9 + 117.4 + 5.7 is 153, but the code never adds the unrounded products. `int()` truncates each one separately, losing up to almost 1 per component.
This is the plain average, (100 + 200 + 50) // 3, the crude method the book replaces. The weights give green, the strongest component here, much more influence.
This is the sum of the components. The weights add up to 1, so the result stays in the 0-255 range of a single component.

questions.hint: Work out each line separately. What does `int()` do to a number such as 29.9?
questions.explanation: The grayscale algorithm multiplies each component by its luminance weight, truncates each product with `int`, adds the three, and stores that luminance in all three components. Because the weights sum to 1, the result is a valid component value.

questions.stem: Why does the book's `grayscale` weight green by .587 and blue by only .114, instead of taking a plain average?

options.text: A plain average would give pure blue the same gray as pure green, though the eye sees blue as darker
options.feedback: The eye is more sensitive to green and red than to blue. Weighting the components by their perceived luminance makes the grays match how bright the colors looked.

options.text: A plain average can exceed 255 for bright pixels, and the weights keep the result in range
options.feedback: The average of three numbers from 0 to 255 is also between 0 and 255. Both methods stay in range; they differ in how much each component counts.

options.text: Green is stored with more bits than blue in the RGB system, so it carries more information
options.feedback: Every RGB component uses the same 8 bits and range. The weights come from human perception, not from how the computer stores the values.

options.text: The weights make the conversion reversible, so the original colors can be restored later
options.feedback: No grayscale conversion is reversible: many different colors map to the same gray. Setting all three components equal throws the color information away.

questions.hint: Imagine a pure blue square next to a pure green one. Do they look equally bright?
questions.explanation: A good grayscale should preserve how light or dark each color *looks*. The human eye is most sensitive to green, then red, then blue, and psychologists measured the relative luminance proportions as .587, .299 and .114, which add up to 1.
questions.aside: The same three weights define the brightness signal (luma) in the ITU-R BT.601 video standard, and before that in the 1953 NTSC color TV system, where that signal let existing black-and-white sets keep showing the picture.

questions.stem: What does this code print?

code.label: Python
code.text:
image = Image(1, 1)
image.setPixel(0, 0, (10, 20, 30))
alias = image
copy = image.clone()
alias.setPixel(0, 0, (0, 0, 0))
print(image.getPixel(0, 0), copy.getPixel(0, 0))

verify.program:
class Image:
    """Stand-in for the book's images.Image: a grid of RGB tuples."""
    def __init__(self, width, height):
        self._w = width
        self._h = height
        self._px = [[(0, 0, 0)] * width for _ in range(height)]
    def getWidth(self):
        return self._w
    def getHeight(self):
        return self._h
    def getPixel(self, x, y):
        return self._px[y][x]
    def setPixel(self, x, y, rgb):
        self._px[y][x] = rgb
    def clone(self):
        new = Image(self._w, self._h)
        new._px = [row[:] for row in self._px]
        return new

image = Image(1, 1)
image.setPixel(0, 0, (10, 20, 30))
alias = image
copy = image.clone()
alias.setPixel(0, 0, (0, 0, 0))
print(image.getPixel(0, 0), copy.getPixel(0, 0))

options.feedback: `alias` is another name for the same image, so changing it changes `image`. `clone()` built a separate image earlier, so `copy` keeps the old pixel.
This treats `alias = image` as making a copy. Assignment never copies an object; it binds a second name to the very same image.
This treats the clone as sharing pixels with the original. `clone()` builds a structurally equivalent image whose pixels are independent of the original's.
This swaps the roles of the two names. The change was made through `alias`, which refers to `image`; `copy` is the only independent object.

questions.hint: How many image objects exist after the third line? After the fourth?
questions.explanation: `clone()` returns a new image with the same width, height and pixels but a separate identity (and an empty filename): structurally equivalent but not identical. Changing pixels in one leaves the other alone. Assignment, by contrast, creates an alias, as with lists in Chapter 5.

questions.concept: Why blur reads from a copy
questions.stem: `blur` reads neighbors from `image` and writes averages into `new = image.clone()`. Suppose it wrote each average back into `image` instead. What would go wrong?

options.text: Neighbors to the left and above would already be blurred when read, skewing each average
options.feedback: In a row-major loop, the pixel on the left and the one above were visited first. Reading their *new* values mixes blurred and original colors, smearing in the loop's direction.

options.text: Nothing: the result is identical, and the program saves the memory of a second image
options.feedback: The result is identical only if every average uses original values. Writing in place changes pixels that later averages still read, so the output differs.

options.text: `setPixel` raises an error when an image is changed while a loop is traversing it
options.feedback: Changing pixels during a traversal is legal: `blackAndWhite` and `grayscale` do exactly that. They are safe because each pixel uses only its own values.

options.text: The pixels on the outer edges would get blurred too, which the original avoids
options.feedback: The edges are skipped by the ranges `1` to `height - 1` and `1` to `width - 1`, not by the copy. Writing in place would not change which pixels are visited.

questions.hint: In a row-major loop, which of a pixel's four neighbors have already been processed when the pixel is reached?
questions.explanation: An algorithm whose result for one pixel depends on its neighbors must read from an unchanged source and write to a separate image. Algorithms that use only the pixel's own values, like grayscale, can safely modify the image in place.
questions.aside: Averaging a pixel with its neighbors equally is called a *box blur*. A Gaussian blur, the default in most photo editors, instead gives nearer pixels more weight, which looks smoother.
questions.ref: Section 8.2, "Blurring an Image" (p. 212) and Exercise 8-2, question 7

questions.stem: `shrink(image, 3)` is applied to an image 600 pixels wide and 300 high. How many pixels does the new image have?

options.text: 20,000, one-ninth of the original
options.feedback: The new image is 600 // 3 by 300 // 3, that is 200 × 100 = 20,000. The original has 180,000, so dividing each dimension by 3 divides the pixels by 3² = 9.

options.text: 60,000, one-third of the original
options.feedback: This divides the total by the factor once. But both the width *and* the height are divided by 3, so the count falls by 3 × 3.

options.text: 180,000, the same as the original
options.feedback: That describes changing the display's resolution, which makes an image look smaller. `shrink` builds a new image with fewer pixels.

options.text: About 6,667, one twenty-seventh of the original
options.feedback: This divides by the factor cubed. An image is two-dimensional, so the factor applies twice, not three times.

questions.hint: Work out the new width and the new height first.
questions.explanation: If the width and height of an image are each reduced by a factor of N, the number of color values falls by a factor of N². `shrink` copies the color of every Nth pixel in every Nth row into the new image, preserving the aspect ratio while throwing information away.
